 A NAS under $300 is best treated as a reliable, low-power file server: centralized storage, automated backups, photo sync, and direct-play media. The ARM processors in this tier aren’t substitutes for a separate x86 compute node when you need broad Docker support or hardware transcoding.
 The three picks here differ in memory, networking, container support, and ease of administration, but all prioritize efficient storage over compute-heavy workloads. Knowing that boundary is the first buying decision. We left out 1 GB models, because 2 GB is the practical floor for current NAS software.
 Our Pick: UGREEN DH2300
 The UGREEN DH2300 ships with 4 GB of RAM and an 8-core ARM processor, double the memory of the other two picks. UGREEN lists it at $269.99.
 CPU: Rockchip 8-core ARM (A72 and A53 cores)
 Memory: 4 GB LPDDR4X, not expandable
 Storage: 2x 3.5”/2.5” SATA bays
 Network and ports: 1x 1GbE, USB-C, two USB-A, 4K HDMI, NFC
 Power: UGREEN advertises about 10W
 Eight cores and 4 GB of memory give the DH2300 more headroom than the quad-core models here for concurrent file transfers, photo thumbnail generation, and media indexing, and less risk of running short of memory under load. HDMI output lets you connect it directly to a display, and NFC makes pairing a phone quick.
 Know what it doesn’t do. UGREEN says the DH2300 does not officially support Docker, and UGREEN’s buying guide says it doesn’t run Plex, Jellyfin, or Emby servers. Memory is fixed, networking is a single gigabit port, and UGOS Pro, UGREEN’s NAS operating system, is the youngest OS in this guide, with fewer community guides than QTS or ADM.
 If the goal is a file server and photo backup target with 4 GB of memory, the DH2300 is the buy. If you need containers, look at the TS-233 or AS3302T below; for a media server, keep compute on a separate mini PC.
 Best 2.5GbE Under $300: ASUSTOR Drivestor 2 Pro Gen2
 The ASUSTOR Drivestor 2 Pro Gen2 (AS3302T v2) is the only pick in this guide with a 2.5GbE port, and it usually costs roughly $280. If your switch and computers support 2.5GbE, it lifts large transfers well beyond the gigabit ceiling of the other two.
 CPU: Realtek RTD1619B, 4-core ARM64, 1.7 GHz
 Memory: 2 GB DDR4, not expandable
 Storage: 2x 3.5”/2.5” SATA bays
 Network and ports: 1x 2.5GbE, 3x USB 3.2 Gen 1
 Rated power: 13.1W in operation, 4.5W with disks hibernating (ASUSTOR)
 2.5GbE raises the ceiling for large sequential transfers from about 112 MB/s on gigabit to roughly 280 MB/s. For video projects, photo library syncs, and full-system restores, the difference is immediately useful.
 ADM (ASUSTOR Data Master) is a capable NAS OS with a clean interface and regular updates. App Central offers Docker Engine and Portainer CE for ARM64 models including this one (ADM 4.3 or later), so a few light containers are possible within 2 GB of memory. Three USB 3.2 ports give you room for external drives, a UPS connection, or USB dongles, and a built-in AES-256 engine handles encrypted shared folders without loading the CPU.
 The limits are the RTD1619B’s modest cores and the fixed 2 GB: no Plex hardware transcoding and no VMs. It costs about $60 more than the TS-233, a fair trade if your network supports 2.5GbE. If you’re still on gigabit, the TS-233 or DH2300 is better value. As with any NAS, keep ADM updated and don’t expose it directly to the internet.
 Budget Pick: QNAP TS-233
 The QNAP TS-233 is the least expensive pick at roughly $220, and it runs QTS, a mature, actively maintained NAS OS with a real app ecosystem.
 CPU: ARM Cortex-A55, 4 cores, 2.0 GHz
 Memory: 2 GB on board, not expandable
 Storage: 2x 3.5”/2.5” SATA bays
 Network and ports: 1x 1GbE, 1x USB 3.2 Gen 1, 2x USB 2.0
 Rated power: 10.8W typical with drives installed, 3.4W in disk standby (QNAP)
 At this price, calibrate expectations. The TS-233 is an excellent file server and backup target: SMB and NFS shares, scheduled backups to USB drives, and Hybrid Backup Sync for other NAS units and cloud storage. QNAP lists volume snapshots for basic data protection. Indexing a large photo library will be slow on 2 GB, but it works.
 Container Station is supported too. QNAP lists Docker and LXD support on the TS-233, with at least 1 GB of RAM required, so a few ARM64 containers are realistic as long as you keep the stack light. Its four Cortex-A55 cores run at 2.0 GHz, versus 1.7 GHz on the ASUSTOR’s RTD1619B.
 QNAP rates the TS-233 at about 10.8W in typical operation with drives installed. At $0.18 per kWh, that is about $17 a year running around the clock, and less when the disks spin down.
 The limits: no Plex hardware transcoding, no Virtualization Station, 2 GB of memory on the board, a single gigabit port, and one USB 3.2 port for expansion. If you need a reliable file server and backup appliance at the lowest practical price, the TS-233 delivers. Keep QTS updated, since QNAP’s security record calls for prompt patching.
 How to Choose: Buying Criteria
 ARM Workload Boundaries
 Every pick here uses an ARM processor. That keeps price and power low, but it sets clear limits:
 Best for file serving, backup, and direct-play media
 ARM64 containers only, on the QNAP and ASUSTOR, and none officially on the UGREEN
 No Plex hardware transcoding
 No practical virtual machines
 Low vendor-rated power, about 10 to 13W in operation
 If your NAS is purely a file server and backup target, these models save money and power. If Docker at scale, VMs, or Plex transcoding are requirements, use our full NAS comparison and raise the hardware budget.
 RAM: The Hidden Bottleneck
 Memory is fixed in every pick, so buy enough for the appliance’s lifetime:
 NAS Ships With Expandable? 
 UGREEN DH2300 4 GB No 
 ASUSTOR AS3302T v2 2 GB No 
 QNAP TS-233 2 GB No 
 The UGREEN’s 4 GB is comfortable for file serving and basic apps. The 2 GB models are tight but workable for their intended use.
 Networking: 1GbE vs 2.5GbE
 At this price, you’re choosing between 1GbE (about 112 MB/s) and 2.5GbE (about 280 MB/s). The practical impact depends on the workload:
 Small file transfers (documents, code repos): No difference. Both feel instant.
 Large file transfers (video, photos, backups): 2.5GbE cuts wait times by about 60%. A 50 GB backup takes about 7.5 minutes on 1GbE and about 3 minutes on 2.5GbE.
 Media streaming : Even 4K HDR remuxes (80+ Mbps) fit well within 1GbE, so you don’t need 2.5GbE for streaming.
 Multi-client access : 1GbE becomes a bottleneck sooner when several users hit the NAS at once.
 The ASUSTOR AS3302T v2 has 2.5GbE; the other two are 1GbE. If you regularly move large files and your network supports 2.5GbE, the improvement is worth paying for.
 Software Ecosystem: QTS vs ADM vs UGOS
 QNAP QTS (TS-233): Feature-rich but more complex. Container Station works on the TS-233 for light ARM64 containers. QNAP’s security history is weaker, so keep auto-update enabled.
 ASUSTOR ADM (AS3302T v2): Clean, capable, regularly updated. Docker Engine and Portainer CE are available in App Central. The app library and community are smaller than DSM’s or QTS’s.
 UGREEN UGOS Pro (DH2300): The newest platform, with a modern mobile app and strong photo backup. No official Docker support on this model, and the smallest third-party ecosystem.
 Bottom Line
 For the most hardware for file storage, the UGREEN DH2300 delivers an 8-core CPU and 4 GB of RAM at a $269.99 list price. Just don’t buy it for Docker or a Plex server.
 If 2.5GbE matters, the ASUSTOR AS3302T v2 is the only pick here with it, and it runs light ARM64 containers through Portainer CE.
 For the lowest price, the QNAP TS-233 runs QTS with Container Station, gets regular security updates, and has a low vendor-rated power draw.
 Ready to see what a bigger budget gets you? Our full NAS comparison covers 4-bay models and beyond.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best NAS under $300? The UGREEN DH2300, listed by UGREEN at $269.99, offers the most CPU cores and memory for file storage and photo backup. Choose the ASUSTOR AS3302T v2 (roughly $280) when 2.5GbE matters, or the QNAP TS-233 (roughly $220) when you want the lowest price and Docker support.
 Can you run Docker on a cheap NAS? Yes, within limits. The QNAP TS-233 runs Docker through Container Station, and the ASUSTOR AS3302T v2 offers Docker Engine and Portainer CE, both for ARM64 images. With 2 GB of memory, plan for a few light services. The UGREEN DH2300 does not officially support Docker. For broad Docker use, budget for an x86 model with more memory.
 Is an ARM NAS worth buying in 2026? Yes, if your needs are file storage, backup, and photo sync. ARM NAS units like the QNAP TS-233 and UGREEN DH2300 are efficient always-on file servers. They fall short for heavy Docker use, Plex hardware transcoding, and virtual machines.
 Which NAS under $300 has 2.5GbE? In this guide, the ASUSTOR Drivestor 2 Pro Gen2 (AS3302T v2). The other picks use 1GbE, which is enough for backups and basic file serving but caps a single transfer near 112 MB/s.
 How much RAM does a budget NAS need? 2 GB is adequate for simple file serving and scheduled backups. 4 GB gives more headroom for indexing, photo apps, and several users. Memory is fixed in all three picks, so choose the UGREEN DH2300 if the extra headroom matters and you don't need Docker.

 You don't need to spend $500 on a NAS enclosure. The best budget NAS devices deliver 2.5G Ethernet, solid backup software, and reliable 24/7 operation for under $300 — drives sold separately.
 Budget NAS devices have improved dramatically over the past few years. Where $200-$300 once bought a slow ARM chip with 512MB of RAM and basic file-sharing support, that same price range now covers dual-core and quad-core ARM processors, Intel N95 and N100 efficiency chips, 2.5G Ethernet ports, and mature software ecosystems. You can build a very capable home NAS without approaching the $500-$700 range that four-bay and performance-focused units occupy.
 This guide focuses exclusively on enclosure prices. Drives are sold separately for all of these units, and that cost deserves its own section below.

 What You Actually Get Under $300: Managing Expectations
 Under $300, the tradeoffs are predictable and manageable once you know what they are.
 Two bays only. Every NAS in this price range is a 2-bay device. That means a maximum of two hard drives, which is enough for RAID 1 mirroring or JBOD (Just a Bunch of Disks) for maximum capacity. If you need four or more bays for a large media library or RAID 5, you are looking at a different price tier.
 1GbE is still common at the low end. The TerraMaster F2-424 and UGREEN DXP2800 stand out by offering 2.5G Ethernet at around $250-$280. The Synology DS223, QNAP TS-233, and TerraMaster F2-212 all ship with standard gigabit Ethernet, which is sufficient for most backup and file-sharing tasks but limits peak transfer speeds to roughly 100-110 MB/s.
 ARM vs Intel CPUs. Three of the five picks here use ARM Cortex-A55 processors. These are efficient, quiet, and handle file sharing, Time Machine, and rsync backups without breaking a sweat. They cannot do hardware video transcoding, and Docker container support is limited. The Intel N95 and N100 chips in the TerraMaster F2-424 and UGREEN DXP2800 change the equation: Intel Quick Sync handles hardware transcoding, and Docker works well.
 RAM is typically 2-4GB and often not expandable. Budget units ship with 2GB DDR4 in most cases. That is fine for file serving and backups, but heavier workloads like simultaneous Docker containers or running VMs require more RAM, which often means stepping up to a different model.
 ARM vs Intel CPU in a Budget NAS: What It Means for You
 The CPU difference in a NAS matters more than the brand on the case. Here is the practical breakdown.
 ARM Cortex-A55 (Synology DS223, QNAP TS-233, TerraMaster F2-212): These processors are power-efficient and perfectly adequate for the primary NAS use cases: Samba file sharing, Time Machine backups, Windows File History via SMB, rsync jobs, and photo storage. Synology's Moments and Photos apps run fine on the DS223. The limitation is transcoding — streaming a video to a device that cannot direct play the format requires software transcoding, which is slow and limits you to one stream at modest quality.
 Intel N95 / N100 (TerraMaster F2-424, UGREEN NASync DXP2800): Intel's Alder Lake N-series efficiency processors bring a major upgrade. Intel Quick Sync hardware transcoding handles 4K H.264 and H.265 decoding, which is a real difference for Plex or Jellyfin users. Docker containers for applications like Home Assistant, AdGuard Home, or Nextcloud run much more reliably. For around $250-$280, the TerraMaster F2-424 and UGREEN DXP2800 offer capabilities that traditionally lived in the $400+ tier.
 2.5G Ethernet at $250: Is the TerraMaster F2-424 Worth It Over Synology?
 The TerraMaster F2-424 costs about $50 more than the Synology DS223 and brings two meaningful upgrades: a 2.5G Ethernet port and an Intel N95 processor. The Synology DS223 sticks with 1GbE and an ARM chip but runs DSM 7 — arguably the best NAS software available.
 In practice, this comes down to your priorities. The TerraMaster F2-424 wins on hardware per dollar. Intel hardware transcoding, 2.5G network throughput (up to ~280 MB/s when paired with a 2.5G switch and compatible computer), and better Docker support make it the performance leader in this price bracket. TOS (TerraMaster Operating System) has improved but still lags DSM in app ecosystem depth and polish.
 The Synology DS223 wins on software. DSM 7 is mature, regularly updated, has a deep app ecosystem (Hyper Backup, Surveillance Station, Drive, Photos, Moments), and is the easiest NAS to manage for non-technical users. If long-term reliability, software quality, and ease of use matter most, the DS223 is worth the hardware compromise.
 The Real Cost: Budget NAS Enclosure Plus Drives
 The enclosure price is only part of what you will spend. A NAS without drives is a box. Here is the realistic total-cost math.
 A pair of 8TB Seagate IronWolf NAS drives typically costs $160-$180 each, putting the drive pair at $320-$360. Add the enclosure cost:
 TerraMaster F2-424 (~$250) + 2x8TB IronWolf: Total system cost roughly $570-$610
 UGREEN DXP2800 (~$280) + 2x8TB IronWolf: Total system cost roughly $600-$640
 Synology DS223 (~$200) + 2x8TB IronWolf: Total system cost roughly $520-$560
 For comparison, a Synology DS224+ (the Intel-based upgrade from the DS223) at around $300 plus the same drives lands at $620-$660 — only $50-$100 more than the DS223 build, but with a meaningful CPU upgrade and 2GB more RAM. If you are near the DS223 option, it is worth pricing out the DS224+ before committing.
 If budget is a hard ceiling and you just need reliable home backups with modest capacity, 4TB drives cut the drive cost roughly in half. Two 4TB IronWolf drives run $70-$90 each, bringing total system cost for a DS223 build to around $340-$380.
 Setting Up a Budget NAS for the First Time: What to Expect From TOS and QTS Lite
 Synology's DSM 7 is widely considered the gold standard for NAS software. Initial setup involves connecting the NAS to your router, opening a browser to find.synology.com, and following a straightforward wizard. Time Machine and Windows File History are configured from the control panel, and shared folders are accessible from any device on the network within minutes of first boot.
 TerraMaster's TOS (TerraMaster Operating System) has evolved considerably and now supports most core NAS functions: shared folders, user accounts, RAID management, Docker, and a growing app store. The interface is less polished than DSM and the app library is smaller, but it covers everything most home users need. TOS setup follows a similar browser-based wizard process.
 QNAP's QTS is feature-rich but sometimes overwhelming. QNAP builds in many security features and advanced networking options that DSM makes optional. For a first NAS, QTS takes slightly more time to configure correctly — particularly around disabling unnecessary remote access features and setting up proper user accounts. The payoff is flexibility: QTS supports a wide range of apps and containers.
 UGREEN's UGOS (UGREEN OS) is the newest software platform on this list. It has improved rapidly and covers the basics well, but the app ecosystem is still developing compared to Synology and QNAP.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is a $200 NAS good enough for home backups?
 Yes — even an ARM-based NAS handles Time Machine, Windows File History, and rsync reliably for a household. The Synology DS223 at around $200 runs full DSM 7 and has excellent app support for backup workflows. You will not feel constrained for standard backup use cases.
 Can a budget NAS run Plex?
 Only reliably with direct play. Software transcoding on ARM or low-end Intel CPUs is limited to 1-2 streams at modest quality. If you need reliable transcoding, the TerraMaster F2-424 or UGREEN DXP2800 with Intel N95/N100 offer hardware transcoding via Intel Quick Sync, which handles 4K H.264 and H.265 decoding. ARM-based picks like the DS223 are better suited to direct-play Plex setups where client devices handle decoding themselves.
 What is the difference between the Synology DS223 and DS224+?
 The DS224+ uses an Intel Celeron J4125 with faster performance, hardware transcoding, and 2GB of RAM expandable to 6GB. The DS223 uses an ARM-based Realtek RTD1619B with lower power draw and a lower price. Both run DSM 7 with the full Synology software ecosystem. The DS224+ handles heavier workloads — transcoding, multiple simultaneous users, Docker containers — significantly better than the DS223.
 Do budget NAS devices support RAID?
 Yes — all NAS devices on this list support RAID 0, RAID 1, and JBOD. RAID 1 mirrors your data across both drives for redundancy, meaning you keep working if one drive fails. RAID 0 stripes data across both drives for faster performance but no redundancy. JBOD presents both drives as separate volumes. Remember that RAID is not a backup — it only protects against a single drive failure, not accidental deletion, fire, theft, or ransomware.

 Rules for Choosing a 2 -Bay NAS
 1 Choose 2-bay when your total data footprint is under 6TB and annual growth is moderate (under 1TB/year). 
 2 Always use CMR (Conventional Magnetic Recording) hard drives to ensure healthy RAID rebuilds without write-cliff failures. 
 3 Remember that a RAID 1 mirror provides uptime redundancy against 1 physical disk failure, but does NOT protect against malware, file deletion, fire, or flood. Maintain an independent off-site 3-2-1 backup. 
 4 If you plan to store more than 12TB or want to host multiple virtual machines, a 4-bay NAS is far more economical per usable terabyte. 
 Mistakes to Avoid Before Buying
 ✕ Buying SMR (Shingled Magnetic Recording) drives which suffer severe write timeouts during RAID rebuilds. 
 ✕ Assuming 2 × 8TB drives equal 16TB of protected space (RAID 1 mirrors data identically, yielding exactly 8TB usable). 
 ✕ Placing 7200rpm high-capacity enterprise drives directly on a resonance-prone wooden desk without vibration dampening. 
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best 2-bay NAS to buy in 2026?
 For most home users, the Synology DS225+ offers the best overall balance of mature backup software, 2.5GbE networking, and automatic phone photo backup. For budget buyers seeking 4K Plex hardware transcoding, the UGREEN DXP2800 with Intel N100 delivers superior raw hardware specifications.
 How much does a 2-bay NAS cost with hard drives?
 Use the cost table on this page for the exact enclosure and drive models. Disk capacity can change the total substantially, and recorded prices can differ from checkout. Add tax, shipping, an independent backup destination, and any UPS or networking you need.
 Can a 2-bay NAS stream and transcode 4K Plex movies?
 Direct Play depends on client support and network bandwidth. For transcoding, an Intel iGPU can help on a supported Plex setup with Plex Pass, but codecs, HDR tone mapping, subtitles, and software versions determine the result. Bay count alone tells you nothing about conversion performance.
 Is a 2-bay NAS better than a 4-bay NAS?
 A 2-bay NAS has a lower upfront entry price and compact desktop footprint. However, a 4-bay NAS is significantly more cost-effective per usable terabyte because RAID 5 achieves 75% storage efficiency compared to only 50% in a 2-bay RAID 1 mirror.
 Can I upgrade to larger hard drives in a 2-bay NAS later without losing data?
 Yes. In a 2-bay mirrored array (SHR or RAID 1), you replace one drive with a larger disk, wait for the storage pool to rebuild, then replace the second drive and expand the volume capacity in your NAS control panel.

 Who a 2-bay NAS is for
 A 2-bay NAS is the entry point to home storage and suits people whose main goals are backups and a private photo cloud. With two drives you can run a mirror, where the same data is written to both disks, so if one fails the other keeps your files safe while you replace it. The trade-off is capacity: a mirror gives you only half the raw storage, because the second drive is a copy rather than extra space.
 That makes a 2-bay ideal for phone photo backup, document storage and syncing files between devices, and acceptable for light media streaming if you pick an Intel model. It is less suited to a fast-growing Plex library or a home lab, where the limited bay count means you run out of room sooner and have fewer options for redundancy.

 Buy the NAS and the drives together, because with only two bays the drives still often cost as much as the enclosure. The headline price you see is for an empty box, so add two NAS-rated CMR drives such as WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf or Toshiba N300 to get a working figure.

 Frequently asked questions
 Why does a 2-bay only give me half the storage?
 In a mirror, the second drive holds an identical copy of the first so your data survives a single drive failure. That protection costs capacity: two four-terabyte drives give four terabytes usable, not eight. If you want more usable space and redundancy together, step up to a 4-bay.
 Can I run Plex on a 2-bay NAS?
 An Intel 2-bay such as the DXP2800, DS224+ or TS-264 runs Plex and handles direct play and light transcoding fine. ARM models like the DH2300 and TS-233 can serve Plex for direct play but struggle to transcode, so avoid them if your TVs or phones need on-the-fly conversion.
 Should I run two drives as a mirror or as one big volume?
 Most home users should mirror, so a single drive failure does not lose data. Combining both drives into one large non-redundant volume gives more space but no protection, which is risky for irreplaceable photos. Only do that if you have a solid separate backup.
 Do the M.2 NVMe slots on a 2-bay help?
 On models like the DXP2800 and TS-264 the NVMe slots can act as a fast cache or, on some platforms, a separate fast pool. For a basic backup and photo workload they are a nice extra rather than essential, but they are useful if you later run more demanding apps.
 Is a 2-bay enough to last me a few years?
 If your needs are backups, documents and a phone photo cloud, yes. If you expect a large media library or a home lab, you may outgrow two bays sooner than you think, and a 4-bay gives far more room and redundancy options for not a great deal more money once drives are counted.

I Built a Silent 2.5GbE NAS on an N100 Mini PC for Under $300 | JPK.io Home Lab I Built a Silent 2.5GbE NAS on an N100 Mini PC for Under $300
 by Joule P. Kraft · August 21, 2026 · updated October 22, 2026 
 As an Amazon Associate, and through other affiliate programs (including SONOFF), I earn from qualifying purchases. No affiliate relationship influences my recommendations.
 I have talked a lot of people out of buying a $600 four-bay NAS. Not because those boxes are bad, but because most people who think they need one actually need a quiet, low-power computer that shares some disks over a fast network, and you can build exactly that for a fraction of the price. This is the build log for the one I run: a Beelink EQ12 N100 mini PC turned into a silent 2.5GbE NAS that idles at under 10 watts, cost me under $300 all in, and has served every file in my house for the better part of a year without a hiccup.
 This is not a theoretical parts list. It is what is sitting on my shelf right now, why I chose each piece, the mistakes I made, and the real transfer numbers I get. If you have been eyeing a Synology and wincing at the price, read this first.
 Why I Skipped a Real NAS
 A prebuilt NAS gives you a tidy box, hot-swap bays, and a polished web UI. What it also gives you is a slow, underpowered ARM or Celeron CPU, locked-down firmware, and a price that assumes you will never learn Linux. The moment you want to run a few containers, a reverse proxy, or anything the vendor did not bless, you are fighting the appliance.
 An N100 mini PC flips that. For roughly the price of a bare diskless two-bay NAS you get a genuinely modern quad-core CPU, 16GB of DDR5, an NVMe boot drive, dual 2.5GbE, and a full x86 box that runs any Linux you want. The Beelink EQ12 I used is the canonical example, but the Beelink, GMKtec, and Aoostar N100 boxes are all the same idea. The N100 sips power, idling around 6 to 10 watts, and it is fast enough to saturate a 2.5GbE link while transcoding a stream and running a dozen containers on the side.
 The one thing a mini PC does not give you is a stack of internal drive bays, and that is the real design constraint. I will come back to how I solved that, because it is where most of the thinking in this build went.
 The Parts List
 Here is exactly what is in mine and what each piece costs roughly:
 Beelink EQ12, Intel N100, 16GB DDR5, 500GB NVMe ; check current price before buying. This is the whole computer. The NVMe is the boot and app drive, and the dual 2.5GbE ports mean I can put one on the LAN and one directly to my desktop later if I want. 16GB of RAM is plenty for OpenMediaVault plus a healthy container stack.
 A powered USB 3.0 dual-bay drive dock ; check current price before buying. This is where the storage lives. The critical word is powered: it has its own barrel-jack power supply so the drives are never starved, unlike bus-powered enclosures that brown out under load. Look for one with an ASMedia or JMicron chipset and UASP support.
 Two NAS-rated hard drives , whatever capacity fits your budget. I run a pair of shucked 8TB CMR drives I already had. Buy CMR, not SMR, for a NAS. A NAS drive search filtered to CMR is the safe path.
 A 2.5GbE switch if your existing one is gigabit, which is the actual bottleneck most people miss. My 2.5GbE upgrade guide walks through the cheap managed options.
 Total for the compute plus dock, not counting drives you may already own, depends on component prices; check current price before buying. That is the whole pitch.
 The USB Storage Question, Honestly
 Let me address the objection I know is coming, because I had it too: USB storage for a NAS sounds like a recipe for corruption. It can be, if you do it wrong. Done right, it is completely reliable, and I have a year of uptime to back that up.
 The rules I follow: use a powered dock, never a bus-powered one. Use a dock with a known-good chipset that supports UASP so you get proper SCSI command queuing instead of slow legacy mass-storage mode. Do not run ZFS over USB, because ZFS wants direct disk access and USB abstracts away exactly what ZFS needs to see. And plug the dock into a rear USB 3.0 port directly, not through a hub.
 Follow those and USB 3.0 gives you about 400 MB/s of theoretical bandwidth, far more than the ~200 MB/s a spinning disk sustains, so USB is not your bottleneck and neither is the disk saturating 2.5GbE the real limit. If you want internal SATA instead, some mini PCs have a 2.5-inch bay, but you are then limited to slow laptop drives or expensive high-capacity 2.5-inch disks. The powered USB dock lets me run full-size 3.5-inch NAS drives, which is the right call for capacity per dollar.
 The Software: Why OpenMediaVault
 I went back and forth on this and landed firmly on OpenMediaVault over TrueNAS Scale for a box like this. TrueNAS is superb, but it is built around ZFS, and ZFS on an N100 with 16GB of non-ECC RAM over USB drives is fighting the tool’s design. ZFS wants ECC memory, direct SATA access, and matched drives in a vdev. None of that describes a mini PC with a USB dock.
 OpenMediaVault is Debian under a clean web UI. It happily runs on modest hardware, formats my drives as EXT4, and shares them over SMB and NFS with a few clicks. Because it is just Debian, I have full apt access, and the OMV-Extras plugin drops in Docker and Portainer so my container stack lives right on the same box. Installation is a standard Debian netinstall followed by the OMV install script, and you are in the web UI in about twenty minutes.
 My setup: the NVMe holds Debian, OMV, and all my Docker volumes. The two USB drives are one big data pool, one for active shares and one that receives a nightly rsync snapshot of the first, so I have on-box versioned backups in addition to my offsite. SMB shares handle the Windows and Mac clients, NFS feeds my Proxmox mini PC and media boxes. It is boring and it just works, which is the goal.
 Real-World Speed
 Numbers, because a build log without them is marketing. All of this is over 2.5GbE through a managed switch, measured with real file copies, not synthetic benchmarks.
 Large sequential transfers, like moving a folder of video files from my desktop to the NAS, run at a steady 270 to 285 MB/s . That is essentially 2.5GbE line rate, and it is limited by the network, not the disk or the USB dock, exactly as it should be. A single 20GB file lands in a little over a minute. Reading back is the same. This is roughly triple what the same setup did on the gigabit switch it replaced, and the difference is immediately obvious when you are shuffling large media around.
 Small-file performance, thousands of tiny files, is slower and always will be on spinning disks, landing in the 40 to 80 MB/s range depending on the file sizes. That is a hard-drive reality, not a fault of this build, and it is why my container app data lives on the NVMe rather than the spinning pool. Power draw sits at 8 to 11 watts at idle with the drives spun down, climbing to about 22 watts under a full transfer with both disks active. Over a year that is a couple of dollars of electricity, versus the space heater some people call a home server.
 What I Would Change
 Two honest notes after a year. First, if I were buying drives fresh instead of using ones I had, I would seriously consider a mini PC with a real internal SATA or a proper DAS enclosure with more bays, purely for tidiness. The USB dock works flawlessly but it is a second box with its own power brick, and a cleaner single-chassis solution has appeal. Second, I would spec a box with an NVMe slot to spare so I could add an SSD cache or a second app drive. The EQ12 has one slot, and it is full. Neither of these is a real complaint, just the things I think about when someone asks what I would do differently.
 The Bottom Line
 You do not need to overspend on an appliance to have a fast, quiet, reliable NAS. An N100 mini PC , a powered USB dock, a pair of CMR drives, and OpenMediaVault gets you a silent, 8-watt-idle, 2.5GbE-saturating file server; check current price before buying. Mine has run for a year without a single unplanned reboot, serves every device in the house at line rate, and doubles as my container host.
 If you have the drives already, the whole project is an afternoon and the price of the mini PC and a dock . Pair it with a cheap 2.5GbE switch so the network is not the bottleneck, install OpenMediaVault, and you have the NAS most people should have built in the first place. It is the most useful $300 in my entire home lab.
 Where to Buy
 Beelink EQ12 N100 mini PC on Amazon Buy on Amazon → USB 3.0 SATA hard drive dock on Amazon Buy on Amazon → NAS hard drives on Amazon Buy on Amazon → 2.5GbE network switches on Amazon Buy on Amazon → As an Amazon Associate, and through other affiliate programs (including SONOFF), we earn from qualifying purchases. Prices and availability are subject to change.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is an N100 mini PC powerful enough to run a NAS? + For a home NAS serving files, media, and a handful of containers, yes, easily. The Intel N100 has four modern cores, handles 2.5GbE line-rate SMB transfers without breaking a sweat, and idles around 6 to 10 watts. It will not replace a big ZFS server with dozens of drives, but for saturating a 2.5GbE link to a few disks it has plenty of headroom, and it does it silently and cheaply.
 Why 2.5GbE instead of 10GbE for a home NAS? + 2.5GbE hits the sweet spot in 2026. It runs over the Cat5e you already have in the walls, the NICs are built into cheap mini PCs like the N100 boxes, and it moves about 280 MB/s, which is faster than a single spinning disk can sustain anyway. 10GbE means new switches, hotter SFP+ gear, and often new cabling for a speed your hard drives cannot feed. For a spinning-disk NAS, 2.5GbE is the right target.
 TrueNAS or OpenMediaVault on an N100 mini PC? + OpenMediaVault is the better fit for a mini PC with a couple of USB or SATA drives. It is Debian-based, light on RAM, and does not demand ECC memory or a specific ZFS topology. TrueNAS Scale is excellent but it really wants ECC RAM and multiple matched drives to shine, which is not what a small N100 box is. I run OMV on mine and it is rock solid.
 Can I use USB drives for a NAS or do I need internal SATA? + USB 3.0 works fine for a home NAS if you use a quality powered dock or enclosure with a stable chipset, and it is often the only option in a tiny mini PC. The main caveats are to avoid the cheapest no-name enclosures that drop connections, and to not run ZFS over USB. For an EXT4 or Btrfs share over USB 3.0 on OMV, it is reliable and easily saturates 2.5GbE.

Best Home NAS 2026: Top Picks for Backup, Plex & Photos | Zen Tech Hub Skip to content 
 Quick answer
 What is the best NAS for home use in 2026?
 UGREEN's NASync DXP4800 Plus wins as the best NAS for home if you want the strongest hardware per pound, especially for Plex. Synology's DS925+ still wins on polished, set-and-forget software for backups and family photos. The real choice in 2026 is aggressive hardware versus mature software.
 Advertisement 
 The best NAS for home use in 2026 comes down to one genuinely interesting fight: UGREEN ’s aggressive hardware versus Synology’s mature software. Two years ago this guide would have been four Synology boxes and a shrug. Then UGREEN started shipping four-bay units with DDR5, 10GbE and desktop-class Intel chips for less than Synology charges for an ARM-adjacent box — and Synology spent a chunk of 2025 annoying its own fans with a third-party drive lockdown it has only partially walked back in DSM 7.3.
 So the honest answer to “which NAS should I buy?” now depends on what you value. If you want the strongest hardware per pound or dollar — especially for Plex — UGREEN’s NASync DXP4800 Plus is our top pick. If you want the most polished, set-and-forget software for backups and family photos, Synology ’s DiskStation DS925+ is still the box to beat. We’ve ranked four units below, based on spec-level research, long-term owner reports and the current state of both software platforms, plus the drive you should put in whichever one you buy.
 For a deeper head-to-head on the two brands, see our full comparison: Synology vs UGREEN NAS (2026): DSM or Raw Power? .
 Comparison Table: The Best Home NAS at a Glance
 Model Bays CPU RAM (base/max) Networking Transcoding iGPU Price (US/UK) 
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus — Best overall 4 (+2 M.2) Intel Pentium Gold 8505 (5-core) 8GB DDR5 / 64GB 10GbE + 2.5GbE Yes around $600 / £560 
 Synology DS925+ — Best software 4 (+2 M.2) AMD Ryzen V1500B (4-core) 4GB DDR4 ECC / 32GB 2x 2.5GbE No around $640 / £520 
 Synology DS225+ — Best 2-bay for beginners 2 Intel Celeron J4125 (4-core) 2GB / 6GB 2.5GbE + 1GbE Yes around $300 / £280 
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800 — Best budget 2 (+2 M.2) Intel N100 (4-core) 8GB DDR5 / 16GB 2.5GbE Yes around $260 / £240 
 Prices move around, especially with UGREEN’s frequent flash sales — check current listings before you buy.
 How We Evaluate a Home NAS
 A NAS is a five-to-ten-year purchase that sits in a cupboard holding your family photos, so we weight things differently than we would for a laptop. Four criteria drive our rankings.
 Software first. The operating system is what you’ll actually live with: backup scheduling, photo indexing, mobile apps, permissions, security updates. A brilliant chassis with clunky software is a bad NAS. This is where Synology’s DSM has historically towered over everyone, and where UGREEN’s UGOS Pro is closing the gap fast.
 Transcoding capability. If Plex or Jellyfin is part of your plan, the CPU’s integrated graphics matter more than core count. Intel chips with Quick Sync can transcode 4K HEVC streams with barely any effort; AMD’s embedded Ryzen chips in current Synology Plus models can’t hardware-transcode at all.
 Upgrade path. Can you add RAM? Are there M.2 slots for cache or SSD volumes? Can you go from two drives to four, or add 10GbE later? A NAS that grows with you beats one you replace in three years.
 Noise, power and reliability. These live in bedrooms and living rooms. In our research we lean heavily on aggregated owner reports for fan noise, drive vibration and long-term failure patterns — the stuff spec sheets never mention.
 Advertisement 
 Best Home NAS Overall: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
 Around $600 / £560 (diskless) 
 The DXP4800 Plus is the reason this category got exciting again. For roughly the price of Synology’s DS925+, UGREEN gives you a 5-core Intel Pentium Gold 8505 (a 12th-gen Alder Lake chip with a proper Iris-class iGPU), 8GB of DDR5 expandable to 64GB, two M.2 NVMe slots, an SD card reader, HDMI 4K output — and both a 10GbE and a 2.5GbE port. On paper, nothing else near this price is close. It’s the best 4-bay NAS for most homes in 2026.
 That hardware translates directly into real-world headroom. The Quick Sync iGPU chews through multiple 4K transcodes in Plex or Jellyfin, the 10GbE port means photo and video editors can work off the NAS at near-local speeds (with a compatible switch or direct connection), and 64GB of RAM capacity makes this a legitimate home-lab box for Docker containers and virtual machines — not just a file server.
 The honest caveat is UGOS Pro. UGREEN’s operating system has matured impressively since launch — snapshots, proper backup tools, a genuinely good photo app with AI-powered search, and Docker support are all present — but it’s still years younger than DSM. Based on hundreds of owner reports, the core experience is now solid and stable; it’s the depth that’s missing. There’s no true equivalent of Synology’s Active Backup suite, third-party app selection is thinner, and power users often end up installing TrueNAS or Unraid on it instead (which UGREEN, to its credit, openly permits without voiding the warranty).
 Who it’s for: Plex households, photographers and tinkerers who want maximum hardware for the money and are comfortable with a good-but-younger OS — or who plan to run their own.
 Pros: 
 Class-leading hardware: DDR5, 5-core Intel with strong iGPU, 64GB RAM ceiling
 10GbE plus 2.5GbE built in — no other sub-$700 4-bay does this
 Excellent Plex/Jellyfin transcoding via Quick Sync
 Two M.2 slots usable for cache or fast SSD volumes
 UGREEN allows third-party OS installs without killing the warranty
 Cons: 
 UGOS Pro still trails DSM in backup depth and app ecosystem
 Shorter track record — UGREEN has been making NAS for ~3 years, not 20
 Fans are audible under sustained load, per owner reports
 Verdict: The best home NAS of 2026 on raw value. Unless best-in-class software is your top priority, buy this.
 Check price: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
 Check price on Amazon → 
 Amazon United States · commission may be earned
 Best Software Experience: Synology DiskStation DS925+
 Around $640 / £520 (diskless) 
 If the DXP4800 Plus is the best hardware, the DS925+ is the best product . Synology’s DSM 7.3 remains the gold standard NAS operating system: Hyper Backup for versioned, encrypted backups to anywhere; Active Backup for Business protecting entire PCs and Microsoft 365 accounts at no extra cost; Synology Photos, which is the closest thing to a self-hosted Google Photos replacement that normal humans can run; and Synology Drive for Dropbox-style sync. For a household that wants to set up backups once and never think about them again, nothing else matches it. Read our full evaluation in Synology DS925+ Review: Still the Home NAS to Beat? .
 The 2026 elephant in the room: drives. In 2025 Synology restricted its Plus-series NAS to Synology-branded and “verified” drives, and the backlash was fierce. DSM 7.3 significantly relaxed this — third-party drives from the likes of Seagate and WD now work for pools and key features again — but you may still see verification nags and a few functions (like some M.2-related features) that prefer Synology’s own media. It’s workable now; it just leaves a sour taste, and it’s a big reason UGREEN took our top slot.
 The hardware itself is competent rather than exciting. The AMD Ryzen V1500B is a reliable quad-core with ECC memory support (genuinely nice for data integrity), and dual 2.5GbE ports can be bonded for ~5Gbps aggregate. But there’s no integrated GPU, so hardware transcoding for Plex is off the table — fine if your clients direct-play, a real limitation if they don’t. There’s also no 10GbE option on this generation, which stung long-time fans.
 Who it’s for: Anyone whose NAS priorities are backup, family photo management, and remote access with minimal fiddling — and who values a 20-year software track record over spec-sheet wins. Also the best NAS for photos, full stop, thanks to Synology Photos.
 Pros: 
 DSM is still the most complete, polished NAS OS available
 Active Backup + Hyper Backup: unmatched free backup suite
 Synology Photos is the best self-hosted photo experience for families
 ECC memory support; quiet, efficient, proven platform
 DSM 7.3 restored broad third-party drive compatibility
 Cons: 
 No iGPU — unsuitable for heavy Plex transcoding
 Weaker, older hardware than UGREEN at a higher US price
 Residual drive-verification warnings on non-Synology disks
 No 10GbE upgrade path
 Verdict: The best NAS for beginners who want it to “just work” for a decade, and the best choice for photo-first households.
 Check price: Synology DiskStation DS925+ 
 Synology DiskStation DS925+
 Check price on Amazon → 
 Amazon United States · commission may be earned
 Best 2-Bay NAS for Beginners: Synology DiskStation DS225+
 Around $300 / £280 (diskless) 
 Most first-time buyers don’t need four bays. Two drives in a mirror (RAID 1), automatic backups from every laptop and phone in the house, and a photo library that isn’t held hostage by a cloud subscription — that’s the whole job, and the DS225+ does it better than any other 2-bay we’ve researched. It’s our pick for the best 2 bay NAS and the easiest on-ramp for a NAS beginner.
 The DS225+ pairs full DSM with an Intel Celeron that — unlike its bigger sibling the DS925+ — includes integrated graphics, so it can hardware-transcode 4K video in Plex or Jellyfin within reason. It also finally brings 2.5GbE to Synology’s small 2-bay line, alongside a 1GbE port. You get the same Synology Photos, Hyper Backup and Drive apps as the flagship models, and DSM’s setup wizard remains the friendliest in the business. If you’re new to all this, our walkthrough covers first-day setup step by step: How to Set Up a NAS: Beginner's Guide (2026) .
 Compromises exist, and you should know them. Base RAM is a slim 2GB (expandable to 6GB — do the upgrade if you’ll run Docker or heavy photo indexing), there are no M.2 slots, and two bays means your expansion story is “buy bigger drives” or “buy a bigger NAS.” That’s fine for backups and a modest media library; it’s limiting if you’re already hoarding 4K remuxes.
 Who it’s for: First-time NAS owners, families replacing Google Photos/iCloud storage tiers, and anyone who wants the Synology experience at half the flagship price.
 Pros: 
 Full DSM experience — same great apps as models twice the price
 iGPU means real Plex hardware transcoding (unlike the DS925+)
 2.5GbE at last in a small Synology
 Compact, quiet, low power draw per owner reports
 Cons: 
 2GB base RAM is tight; max 6GB
 No M.2 slots or meaningful expansion path
 Same lingering third-party drive nags as other 2025/26 Synology models
 Verdict: The default recommendation for a first NAS. Simple, safe, and genuinely pleasant to use.
 Check price: Synology DiskStation DS225+ 
 Synology DiskStation DS225+
 Check price on Amazon → 
 Amazon United States · commission may be earned
 Advertisement 
 Best Budget NAS: UGREEN NASync DXP2800
 Around $260 / £240 (diskless) 
 The DXP2800 is the cheapest NAS we’re comfortable recommending in 2026, and it’s a spec-sheet bully at the price. For less than the Synology DS225+, you get an Intel N100 — a genuinely capable quad-core with Quick Sync graphics — 8GB of DDR5 (four times the Synology’s base RAM), two M.2 NVMe slots, 2.5GbE and an HDMI port that can output your media library directly to a TV. As pure hardware, it embarrasses everything else under $300.
 The trade-off is the same one that runs through this whole guide: software. UGOS Pro covers the essentials well — SMB shares, snapshots, phone photo backup, a Docker app for everything else — but its ecosystem is basic compared to DSM’s. Based on aggregated owner feedback, the most common pattern is buyers using it as a straightforward file/backup target plus a Jellyfin or Plex box via Docker, where it performs beautifully. If you want deep, integrated apps for every task, the Synology 2-bay above is worth the extra money.
 Who it’s for: Budget-conscious buyers, Plex/Jellyfin streamers on a 2-drive budget, and tinkerers who’d rather have the N100’s muscle than a richer app store. The best budget NAS of 2026.
 Pros: 
 Unbeatable hardware per dollar: N100, 8GB DDR5, dual M.2, 2.5GbE
 Hardware transcoding handles multiple 1080p or a couple of 4K streams
 HDMI out for direct-to-TV playback
 Frequently discounted below list price
 Cons: 
 UGOS Pro app ecosystem is the thinnest of our picks
 Single 2.5GbE port, no link aggregation
 Two bays plus M.2 is flexible, but drive expansion is still capped
 Verdict: The most NAS you can get for around $260 / £240 — as long as you’re happy with capable-but-basic software or Docker.
 Check price: UGREEN NASync DXP2800 
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800
 Check price on Amazon → 
 Amazon United States · commission may be earned
 Best NAS for Plex: Which CPUs Actually Matter
 The single most misunderstood part of NAS shopping is transcoding, so here’s the short version. Plex only transcodes when a client can’t play the original file — wrong codec, bandwidth limits, or burned-in subtitles. When that happens, an Intel CPU with Quick Sync (the iGPU in the Pentium Gold 8505, N100 and Celeron J4125 above) handles multiple 4K HEVC conversions with low power draw. AMD’s V1500B in the DS925+ has no iGPU, so every transcode hammers the CPU cores and 4K transcoding is effectively a non-starter.
 Practical guidance from our research:
 Everything direct-plays (Apple TV 4K, Nvidia Shield, modern smart TVs on your LAN): any NAS here works, including the DS925+.
 Remote streaming to phones/browsers, or mixed devices: you want Quick Sync — the DXP4800 Plus is the best NAS for Plex in this guide, with the DXP2800 the budget route.
 Tone-mapped 4K HDR transcodes for several users: DXP4800 Plus, ideally with a Plex Pass for hardware acceleration.
 One more note: Plex’s 2025 price rises pushed many owners to Jellyfin, which is free and runs well in Docker on all four picks — hardware transcoding included on the Intel boxes.
 Don’t Forget the Drives: WD Red Plus vs Seagate IronWolf
 A diskless NAS is a very nice paperweight. Budget for drives from day one, and only buy CMR NAS-rated drives — desktop drives using SMR recording can behave badly in RAID rebuilds.
 Our default recommendation is the Seagate IronWolf 8TB at around $170 / £160 per drive. It’s CMR, rated for 24/7 NAS duty and workloads of 180TB/year, carries a 3-year warranty, and includes three years of Seagate’s Rescue data recovery service — a genuinely useful safety net most buyers don’t know they’re getting. Two of them in RAID 1 gives a beginner 8TB of protected storage; four in RAID 5 or SHR gives you roughly 24TB usable.
 Check price: Seagate IronWolf 8TB 
 WD Red Plus is the equally valid alternative — also CMR, similar pricing, and in owner reports slightly quieter at idle, while IronWolf tends to edge it on sustained performance and includes the recovery service. Honestly, buy whichever is cheaper the day you order; both are proven. What matters more is buying two identical-capacity drives and enabling your NAS’s scheduled SMART tests.
 And the 2026 Synology wrinkle, once more: with DSM 7.3, IronWolf and Red Plus drives work fine in the DS925+ and DS225+ for storage pools, though you may see “unverified drive” notices. Ignore the nag; the drives are fine, and this pairing is exactly what most Synology owners run.
 Advertisement 
 DSM vs UGOS Pro: The Software Gap Explained
 Since the whole synology vs ugreen decision hinges on software, here’s the gap in concrete terms as of mid-2026.
 Where DSM still wins clearly: backup breadth (Active Backup for Business can image entire Windows PCs and back up Microsoft 365/Google Workspace for free), Synology Photos’ face/subject recognition and shared family libraries, the third-party package ecosystem, Surveillance Station for cameras, and two decades of security-response reputation. DSM also has SHR, Synology’s flexible RAID that lets you mix drive sizes efficiently.
 Where UGOS Pro has caught up: the fundamentals. Storage management, snapshots, SMB/NFS performance, mobile photo backup with AI search, remote access, and a proper Docker implementation are all solid now, per widespread owner reports — a big shift from the rough 2024 launch. UGREEN has shipped updates at an impressive cadence.
 Where UGOS Pro still trails: no Active Backup equivalent, fewer native apps (you’ll lean on Docker), less granular permissions for multi-user households, and a shorter security track record. The wildcard: UGREEN officially tolerates third-party operating systems, so a DXP4800 Plus running TrueNAS SCALE or Unraid is a popular power-user path that Synology hardware can’t economically match.
 Our rule of thumb: if you’ll use more than two of Synology’s flagship apps, buy Synology. If you mainly need files, photos, and a media server, UGREEN’s hardware advantage wins.
 How Much NAS Do You Actually Need?
 RAID is not backup. RAID protects against a drive dying, not against ransomware, accidental deletion, or a house fire. Follow 3-2-1: three copies of important data, on two media types, one off-site (a cloud target or a NAS at a relative’s house — both Hyper Backup and UGOS support this).
 Capacity planning: take your current data, double it, then add your annual photo/video growth for five years. For most families that lands at 4–12TB of usable space — comfortably inside a 2-bay with 8TB mirrored drives. Buy a 4-bay when you’re already past ~10TB, you shoot lots of video, or you’re building a serious media library, because migrating later is a chore.
 RAID choices, simply: 2-bay = RAID 1 (mirror, half your raw capacity, one-drive fault tolerance). 4-bay = RAID 5 or Synology SHR (capacity of all drives minus one, one-drive fault tolerance). Skip RAID 0 entirely for anything you care about.
 UK buyers: all four picks are sold and supported in the UK; the DS925+ is notably better value in Britain (around £520) than in the US, while UGREEN’s UK pricing fluctuates with frequent voucher promotions — check both before deciding. For more network gear guides, browse our hub: Networking & Wi-Fi .
 Which Should You Buy?
 Best overall / best for Plex: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus — unmatched hardware, fast-improving software.
 Best software, backups and photos: Synology DS925+ — DSM remains worth paying for if you’ll use it.
 Best first NAS: Synology DS225+ — the friendliest 2-bay on sale.
 Best budget: UGREEN DXP2800 — N100 power at a knockdown price.
 In every case: add two or four Seagate IronWolf 8TB (or WD Red Plus) drives.
 Advertisement 
 FAQ: Home NAS
 What is the best NAS for home use in 2026?
 For most people it’s the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: a 4-bay with a 5-core Intel CPU, DDR5, 10GbE and hardware transcoding for around $600 / £560. If you’d rather have the most polished software for backups and photos than the strongest hardware, the Synology DS925+ is the better buy.
 Is a 2-bay or 4-bay NAS better for home?
 A 2-bay in RAID 1 covers most households: backups, photos and a modest media library, up to roughly 8–16TB usable. Choose a 4-bay if you already store more than ~10TB, want RAID 5/SHR efficiency, or expect a growing Plex library — migrating from a full 2-bay later is tedious.
 Can I use non-Synology drives in a Synology NAS in 2026?
 Yes. DSM 7.3 relaxed the 2025 restrictions, so third-party CMR NAS drives like Seagate IronWolf and WD Red Plus work in current Plus models, including the DS925+ and DS225+. You may still see “unverified drive” notices, and a few M.2-related features prefer Synology media, but storage pools work normally.
 Which NAS is best for Plex?
 One with an Intel CPU featuring Quick Sync graphics. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the strongest Plex NAS in this guide, handling multiple 4K transcodes; the budget DXP2800 and Synology DS225+ also transcode well. Avoid the DS925+ for transcoding-heavy Plex use — its AMD chip has no iGPU.
 Is UGREEN NAS as good as Synology?
 On hardware, UGREEN is better at every price point — newer CPUs, more RAM, faster networking. On software, Synology’s DSM still leads in backup tools, photo management and app depth, though UGOS Pro has matured into a solid daily driver. Buy on software needs, not spec sheets.
 How much should I spend on a home NAS?
 Plan for around $500–1,000 / £450–950 all-in. A budget setup (UGREEN DXP2800 plus two IronWolf 8TB drives) runs roughly $600 / £560 total; a 4-bay DXP4800 Plus or DS925+ with four drives lands near $1,300 / £1,200. Remember the enclosure price never includes drives.

Best 2-Bay NAS (2026): Backups, Plex, Beginners | ComputingForGeeks

 ⓘ This post contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 Before you compare brands, decide whether your 2-bay NAS will only hold backups or will also run Plex. That one answer decides the CPU, the RAM and whether you spend about $210 or about $390. A backup-only box can be a cheap ARM unit that sips power. A media server needs an Intel chip with Quick Sync, and the cheapest models skip it.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 177134 
 We compared six current 2-bay models from Synology, UGREEN and TerraMaster for three kinds of buyer. You want automatic backups of phones and laptops, you want a Plex or Jellyfin server, or you’ve never owned a NAS and want the fewest surprises. Each pick is priced with a mirrored pair of CMR drives, since two drives in RAID 1 give you the capacity of one. This is desk research from vendor spec sheets and cited reviews, not a bench test, and prices and stock below were checked on Amazon on October 24, 2026.
 Best 2-bay NAS picks at a glance
 Start from what the NAS will do for you, not from the spec sheet. Each award below names the job it is best at:
 Best for first-time owners: Synology DS225+ , about $365. DSM is the easiest NAS software to live with, and it carries a three-year warranty.
 Best for Plex and Jellyfin: UGREEN DXP2800 , about $390. An Intel N100 with Quick Sync, 8 GB of DDR5 and two M.2 slots.
 Best budget x86 box: TerraMaster F2-425 , about $255. Quick Sync and 2.5GbE for the price of an ARM box, with a locked OS.
 Best premium pick: UGREEN DXP2800 GT , about $460. The only 10GbE port in this guide and room for 64 GB of RAM.
 Cheapest box for backups: Synology DS223j , about $210. DSM backup tools on a 1 GB ARM box with one gigabit port.
 Lowest power draw: UGREEN DH2300 , about $239. Rated 13.72 W while working, but no Docker and no Plex server.
 Prices move daily, so treat these as the level we saw and check the live listing before you buy. If the box will ever run a media server, skip straight to the DXP2800 or the F2-425, because the two ARM picks and the DS225+ cannot transcode for Plex as shipped.
 How we picked these six
 Every spec in this guide comes from the maker’s own product page, and every price and stock line from Amazon’s catalog API on October 24, 2026. We only kept NAS listings sold by Amazon.com or the brand’s own Amazon storefront, so a warranty claim goes to someone accountable. Speeds, idle power and noise come from the independent reviews linked in each section. We did not bench these units ourselves, and where we found no independent test, we say so.
 We left out boxes we could not verify or buy cleanly, and there is a short list of those near the end. If you’d rather build than buy, our DIY NAS on a mini PC guide prices that route against these boxes.
 2-bay NAS comparison table
 These columns hold the specs that change the decision for a 2-bay buyer. Quick Sync decides Plex, the network port decides copy speed, and the warranty and OS rules decide what happens in year three:
 Model Price on Oct 24, 2026 CPU RAM (max) Network M.2 Quick Sync Warranty 
 Synology DS225+ $364.99 Celeron J4125 2 GB (6 GB) 1GbE + 2.5GbE None Yes, needs a community driver 3 years 
 UGREEN DXP2800 $389.99 Intel N100 8 GB DDR5 (16 GB) 2.5GbE 2x NVMe Yes 2 years 
 TerraMaster F2-425 $254.99 Celeron N5095 4 GB (16 GB) 2.5GbE None Yes 2 years 
 UGREEN DXP2800 GT $459.99 Ryzen Embedded R2514 8 GB DDR4 (64 GB) 10GbE 2x NVMe No (Radeon graphics) 2 years 
 Synology DS223j $209.99 Realtek RTD1619B (ARM) 1 GB (fixed) 1GbE None No 2 years 
 UGREEN DH2300 $239.00 Rockchip 8-core (ARM) 4 GB 1GbE None No 2 years 
 Read the Quick Sync column first. Three boxes have it, and only two of those use it for Plex without extra work, which is why the DS225+ wins for first-time owners but not for media servers. The 1GbE boxes top out near 115 MB/s on copies, so copying 10 TB onto one takes about a day. The 2.5GbE boxes need roughly 10 to 15 hours, depending on how fast each writes.
 Mirrored drives cost more than the box
 A 2-bay NAS almost always runs RAID 1, which writes every file to both drives, so you pay for two drives and get the space of one. That makes the drives the bigger bill. These are the cheapest new CMR NAS drives we found sold by Amazon.com (Adorama for the 6TB), priced as a mirrored pair:
 Drive Price each on Oct 24, 2026 Mirrored pair Usable space Per usable TB 
 WD Red Plus 6TB (sold by Adorama) $299.99 $599.98 6 TB $100.00 
 WD Red Plus 10TB $459.99 $919.98 10 TB $92.00 
 WD Red Pro 12TB $539.99 $1,079.98 12 TB $90.00 
 WD Red Pro 16TB $714.99 $1,429.98 16 TB $89.37 
 WD Red Pro 20TB $907.47 $1,814.94 20 TB $90.75 
 From 10 TB up, the cost per usable TB barely moves, between $89 and $92, so buy the largest pair you can afford now. Two bays cannot grow by adding a third drive. The only upgrade path is replacing both drives with bigger ones, one at a time, with a full rebuild after each swap. The 6TB pair is the worst value per TB here, and it was the smallest new CMR drive we found from a seller we’d trust. No 4TB or 8TB CMR drive was sold by Amazon.com when we checked.
 With a 10TB pair, the full builds land between about $1,130 (DS223j) and $1,380 (DXP2800 GT), which is why a cheaper box rarely changes the total by much. Buy CMR drives only, since SMR drives can stall a rebuild for days. The CMR vs SMR explainer covers why, and our NAS hard drive rankings track more sizes and brands by price per TB.
 1. Synology DS225+
 For someone who has never owned a NAS, the DS225+ is the 2-bay box we’d hand over first. DSM’s backup apps, snapshots and phone photo backup are the most finished software in this guide, and Synology is the only maker here that gives three years of warranty.
 Synology DS225+: Celeron J4125, 1GbE plus 2.5GbE, three-year warranty. Image: Synology. 
 Inside is a four-core Celeron J4125 with 2 GB of DDR4, expandable to 6 GB, two hot-swap bays for up to 48 TB raw, and one 1GbE plus one 2.5GbE port. Synology rates it at 282 MB/s reads, and NASCompares reports up to 280 to 290 MB/s over 2.5GbE, so the faster port is real. Synology rates writes lower, at 217 MB/s. That review also found DSM using 28 to 38% of the RAM at rest, which is the first sign that 2 GB is tight once you add apps.
 The 2025 drive lock is gone too, and that was the big complaint when this model launched. Synology’s DSM 7.3 announcement says 25-series Plus, Value and J models accept non-validated third-party drives for storage pools, so the WD drives above work. Where it falls short:
 Plex transcoding needs a workaround: the DS225+ ships without the i915 modules Plex and Jellyfin use, and the fix is the community Transcode for x25 package .
 No M.2 slots: an SSD cache would cost one of your two drive bays.
 An old CPU: the J4125 dates from 2019, and 6 GB is the RAM ceiling for its whole life.
 Pick it if backups, photo sync and file shares are the job and you want software that needs no tinkering, at about $365 sold by Amazon.com. Look elsewhere if Plex is part of the plan, because running an unofficial driver package on your only copy of the family photos is the opposite of why you’d buy a Synology in the first place.
 Check DS225+ price on Amazon 
 2. UGREEN DXP2800
 For a 2-bay Plex or Jellyfin server, the DXP2800 is the standout. Its Intel N100 has Quick Sync and it ships with 8 GB of DDR5, four times the RAM of the DS225+. It also has the two M.2 slots the Synology lacks, for about $25 more.
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800: Intel N100, 8 GB DDR5, two NVMe slots, 2.5GbE. Image: UGREEN. 
 Intel’s N100 is a four-core chip, and Quick Sync is the transcoding path Plex and Jellyfin support best. That is why this box handles media without any driver workarounds. The RAM sits in one SO-DIMM slot that takes 16 GB, and the network is one 2.5GbE port. The OS boots from a 32 GB eMMC chip, so both bays stay free for data. ocinside measured about 7 W idle , 34.7 W at peak, and 181 MB/s writing to a RAID 1 pair.
 UGREEN’s software, UGOS Pro, is younger than DSM, and you will notice it in the backup and photo apps more than in file sharing. What you give up:
 Noise: UGREEN rates it at 29 to 34 dB in quiet mode, higher than the 19.6 dB(A) Synology quotes for the DS225+, though the two are measured differently.
 Warranty: two years against Synology’s three.
 M.2 speed: the N100 platform runs PCIe Gen 3, so the NVMe slots won’t run Gen 4 drives at full speed.
 It’s also the box that grows with you. In a March 2024 update to NASCompares’ UGREEN Q&A , a UGREEN representative said the warranty covers only the hardware and warned that a third-party OS risks data loss and compatibility issues, though older text on that page still says it voids the warranty. TrueNAS or Unraid later is an option, but get UGREEN’s answer in writing first. Pick it at about $390, sold by UGREEN, if Plex is on the plan. For more media-server boxes beyond two bays, see our NAS picks for Plex and self-hosting .
 Check DXP2800 price on Amazon 
 3. TerraMaster F2-425
 The F2-425 is the cheapest way into an x86 NAS with Quick Sync, at about $255, which is $135 less than the DXP2800 and only $45 more than the ARM-based DS223j. TerraMaster rates its Celeron N5095 for H.264 and H.265 transcoding at 4K60.
 TerraMaster F2-425: Celeron N5095, 4 GB RAM up to 16 GB, 2.5GbE. Image: TerraMaster. 
 You get 4 GB of RAM in a SODIMM slot that takes 16 GB, one 2.5GbE port, two 10Gbps USB ports and HDMI, and bays for up to 60 TB raw. TerraMaster’s product page title says N95 while its spec table says N5095; we’ve gone with the spec table, and so should you when comparing. TerraMaster rates it at 22 W working and 11 W in hibernation, the highest hibernation figure of the budget picks.
 Its low price comes with three conditions you should accept up front:
 The OS is locked: TerraMaster states that installing another system voids the warranty , so this box runs TOS for its whole life.
 An older chip: the N5095 is a 2021 Jasper Lake part, and there is no M.2 slot for a cache.
 Thin stock: Amazon showed 9 units left from TerraMaster’s storefront when we checked.
 Buy it if you want Plex-capable hardware on the smallest budget and you’re happy with TerraMaster’s own software. If the price climbs back toward its $300 list, the DXP2800 is the better buy for the extra RAM and M.2 slots.
 Check F2-425 price on Amazon 
 4. UGREEN DXP2800 GT
 The GT is the 2-bay NAS for a home that already has 10GbE, or plans to. It’s the only box here with a 10GbE port, and its two SO-DIMM slots take up to 64 GB, enough for real VMs next to the file shares.
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800 GT: Ryzen Embedded R2514, 10GbE, up to 64 GB RAM. Image: UGREEN. 
 It runs an AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 with four cores and eight threads at up to 3.7 GHz, ships with 8 GB of DDR4, and has two NVMe slots. The bays also take U.2 drives. Notebookcheck measured 14.84 to 20.14 W idle, 35.9 W at peak, and 29.11 dB(A) idle at 30 cm, and called it surprisingly quiet. One spec doesn’t match the price, though:
 No Quick Sync: the Radeon graphics are not Intel’s encoder, so check your media server’s AMD support before you count on transcoding.
 Power: UGREEN rates it at 42.36 W working and 18.12 W in hibernation, about two and a half times the DXP2800.
 M.2 lanes: Mighty Gadget reports each NVMe slot runs at Gen 3 x2.
 Two bays and 10GbE is an odd pairing, because a mirrored pair of hard drives cannot fill a 10GbE link on its own. The port earns its keep when you put fast NVMe storage in those slots. Pick it at about $460, sold by UGREEN, if you will use the NVMe slots and the RAM; for a plain backup box it’s paying for hardware you’ll never touch.
 Check DXP2800 GT price on Amazon 
 5. Synology DS223j
 If all you want is a place for laptop and phone backups with Synology’s software, the DS223j does it for about $210. It runs the same DSM as the DS225+, including Btrfs, Synology Hybrid RAID and snapshot replication.
 Synology DS223j: Realtek ARM chip, 1 GB RAM, one 1GbE port. Image: Synology. 
 Synology kept the hardware minimal on purpose: a four-core Realtek RTD1619B ARM chip at 1.7 GHz, 1 GB of RAM that cannot be upgraded, and one 1GbE port. StorageReview measured 115 MB/s reads and writes over SMB in RAID 1, which is gigabit line rate, so the drives were never the bottleneck. Synology’s own spec table suggests a ceiling of 5 users in Synology Drive.
 The bays are not hot-swap, so a failed drive means powering the box down before you swap it. The warranty is two years, not three, and there is no Intel Quick Sync, so plan on direct play rather than transcoding. It’s quiet at 18.2 dB(A) and rated at 4 W in hibernation. Buy it as a backup target and nothing more; if you can stretch to the F2-425 for $45 extra, you get x86, Quick Sync and 2.5GbE.
 Check DS223j price on Amazon 
 6. UGREEN DH2300
 Of the six, the DH2300 draws the least power, rated at 13.72 W working and 3.3 W in hibernation, which makes it the cheapest box here to leave on. UGREEN sells it as a beginner’s backup NAS, and it’s honest about the limits.
 UGREEN NASync DH2300: eight-core Rockchip ARM, 4 GB RAM, 1GbE. Image: UGREEN. 
 It pairs an eight-core Rockchip chip (an RK3576, per PCMag’s review ) with 4 GB of RAM, one 1GbE port and bays for up to 64 TB. PCMag measured 107 MB/s writes and 108 MB/s reads, gigabit speed again. UGREEN’s own product page tells you not to buy it for a Plex server or Home Assistant, and there’s no Docker and no VM support. The apps UGREEN ships are the apps you get.
 Against the DS223j, you trade DSM for four times the RAM and a lower power rating, and you pay about $29 more. Stock was thin, with 12 units left from UGREEN’s storefront when we checked. Pick it for a quiet backup box that stays on, at about $239, and pick the DS223j instead if you want Synology’s backup apps.
 Check DH2300 price on Amazon 
 What a 2-bay NAS costs to run for a year
 A home NAS stays on around the clock, so the power rating is a running cost you’ll pay every month. We took each maker’s “access” figure, which is measured with drives working, and ran it for all 8,760 hours of a year at $0.20 per kWh. Scale the last column to your own rate:
 Model Rated access power Rated hibernation kWh per year at access Cost per year at $0.20/kWh 
 UGREEN DH2300 13.72 W 3.30 W 120.2 $24.04 
 Synology DS223j 16.31 W 4.00 W 142.9 $28.58 
 UGREEN DXP2800 16.38 W 5.24 W 143.5 $28.70 
 Synology DS225+ 16.98 W 6.08 W 148.7 $29.75 
 TerraMaster F2-425 22.00 W 11.00 W 192.7 $38.54 
 UGREEN DXP2800 GT 42.36 W 18.12 W 371.1 $74.21 
 Treat these numbers as a worst case. A home NAS spends most of its day idle or with drives spun down, and the reviews above measured lower idle figures than these ratings. Even so, the gap is the useful part. Four of the six cost $24 to $30 a year to run, so power shouldn’t decide between them. The GT costs about $45 a year more than the DXP2800, which adds up to about $228 over five years, three times the $70 gap in their prices.
 What first-time NAS owners should check before buying
 Most first-NAS regrets come from a handful of assumptions that sound reasonable and aren’t. Go through these before you order:
 RAID 1 is not a backup: a mirror survives one dead drive, but a deleted file, ransomware or a fire takes out both copies at once. Keep a second copy off the NAS, on a USB drive or a cloud bucket.
 Two bays means one drive of space: plan capacity for three or four years, because the only way to grow is replacing both drives.
 Plex needs Quick Sync: phones and smart TVs often can’t play every file directly, and without a hardware encoder the NAS can’t convert it on the fly. Since DSM 7.2.2, Synology Photos and its other media apps hand HEVC, AVC and VC-1 to the playing device instead of converting them.
 Gigabit caps copy speed: 1GbE boxes top out near 115 MB/s, which is fine for backups and a bottleneck for editing video off the NAS.
 The OS is part of the purchase: TerraMaster voids the warranty on a third-party OS, Synology runs only DSM, and UGREEN has warned of data-loss risk with a third-party OS.
 Buy CMR drives: SMR drives can turn a routine rebuild into a multi-day crawl, and a 2-bay box has no second parity to fall back on while it runs.
 People skip the first item most often. If the off-NAS copy is a USB disk, our list of external drives for backups covers which ones hold up. The NAS’s own backup app can write to it on a schedule.
 Models left out on purpose
 A few popular 2-bay boxes didn’t make the cut, and the reasons are about buying them, not about the hardware:
 QNAP TS-264: listed at about $469, but the only seller was Adorama with thin stock, and at that price the DXP2800 GT adds 10GbE.
 TerraMaster F2-425 Plus: about $425, but we couldn’t confirm which CPU ships on the current listing, since N150 and N95 versions both exist.
 Four bays: if you want RAID 5 or room to add drives later, our 4-bay NAS guide prices that step up.
 If you’re leaving Synology rather than starting fresh, the Synology alternatives roundup compares the same UGREEN boxes against QNAP, UniFi and DIY builds.
 Where each 2-bay NAS falls short
 No box here is right for every home, so it helps to know the single weakness you’d live with on each:
 Synology DS225+: Plex transcoding needs an unofficial driver package, and RAM stops at 6 GB.
 UGREEN DXP2800: louder than the Synologys, with younger software and a two-year warranty.
 TerraMaster F2-425: any other OS voids the warranty, and stock was down to single digits.
 UGREEN DXP2800 GT: no Quick Sync and the highest power draw. Its 10GbE port is also wasted on a pair of hard drives alone.
 Synology DS223j: 1 GB of fixed RAM, gigabit only, and no hot-swap bays.
 UGREEN DH2300: no Docker, no VMs and no Plex server, by UGREEN’s own description.
 For most first-time owners we’d still start with the DS225+ for backups or the DXP2800 for media, because their weaknesses are the easiest to live with. Whichever you pick, spend the money you save on the box on the biggest CMR pair you can afford, since that’s the part you can’t upgrade without starting over.
